strengths: Simple, low-cost idea (reversing step order via prompting, no added parameters) that is easy to integrate into existing PRM pipelines.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 3 backbones (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Rho-Math-1B, Deepseek-Math-7B), 3 training objectives (BCE, MSE, Q-value ranking), 3 policy/sampling models, and 2 benchmarks (GSM-Plus, MATH500), yielding dozens of configurations with consistent improvements.
Ablation study (w/o L2R, w/o R2L) supports the claim that both directions contribute complementary signal rather than one direction dominating.
Qualitative case study illustrates a plausible mechanism by which backward verification can catch errors that forward-only scoring misses.
The method is framework-agnostic and could be adopted by other PRM training pipelines with minimal overhead.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Eqs. 2 and 6) is somewhat superficial: causal masking trivially yields zero partial derivatives w.r.t. future tokens by construction, and labeling this 'gradient vanishing' overstates the novelty of the diagnosis; the actual mechanism by which reversing step order helps a causal LM (which was never trained on such reversed, out-of-order text) is not carefully analyzed.

No baseline is included to disentangle whether gains stem from genuine bidirectional/backward verification versus simple two-stream ensembling/variance reduction (e.g., averaging two forward passes with different prompts/seeds). This is a critical missing control given the method essentially averages two scalar scores.

Training details for the R2L stream are underspecified: it is unclear whether the shared parameters fθ are trained on both forward and reversed trajectories jointly, or whether R2L scoring is applied zero-shot at inference to a model trained only in the forward direction; this ambiguity affects reproducibility and interpretation of results.

The claim of 'zero inference latency' is optimistic; while no new parameters are added, running two full forward passes through the same-sized backbone at minimum doubles compute/memory cost unless extra parallel hardware is available, and this trade-off is not discussed or measured.

No variance/error bars or repeated-seed results are reported despite many close-margin comparisons (differences of ~1-3 points in several configurations), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

The 'bidirectional' framing (analogy to BiLSTM) is somewhat of a stretch: the underlying model remains autoregressive/causal in each direction, so this is more accurately described as a dual-pass ensembling scheme over reversed step order rather than a jointly bidirectional architecture.

Comparisons to simpler alternative baselines (e.g., self-consistency, majority voting, or straightforward two-sample ensembling of standard L2R PRMs) are absent, limiting the ability to judge whether the specific 'reversed reasoning' mechanism is necessary for the observed gains.

strengths: The proposed idea (adding a parallel right-to-left evaluation stream via prompt reversal, with no extra parameters and no additional inference latency) is simple, lightweight, and easy to integrate into existing PRM pipelines.

Experimental coverage is broad: 3 backbones (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Rho-Math-1B, Deepseek-Math-7B) x 3 training objectives (BCE, MSE, Q-value ranking) x 2 benchmarks (MATH500, GSM-Plus) x 3 sampling policies, totaling 54 configurations, with consistent improvements in every setting reported, which suggests the effect is not a fluke of one setup.
Ablation studies (w/o L2R, w/o R2L, full BiPRM) show both directions individually underperform the fused model, supporting the claim that combining both directions is useful.

The paper is clearly written, with a reasonable motivating example (mathematical induction case) and a qualitative case study illustrating differing reward trajectories between BiPRM and L2R-only scoring.
Full per-n results are reported in appendices, aiding transparency of the numeric claims.
weaknesses: The exact training procedure for BiPRM is underspecified: Section 3.2 presents the fused reward only as an inference-time formula (Eq. 4), while Section 3.3 describes the loss functions generically without clarifying whether the shared parameters fθ are trained on both forward and reversed trajectories jointly, or whether BiPRM is simply a standard L2R-trained model applied post hoc to reversed sequences at test time. This ambiguity is central to interpreting why the shared reward head generalizes to the R2L direction and needs to be resolved for reproducibility.

No control baseline is provided to rule out a simple ensembling/variance-reduction explanation for the gains: averaging two scores from the same forward-direction model (e.g., via dropout or multiple forward passes) could plausibly also improve Best-of-N accuracy by reducing noise, independent of any genuine 'backward verification' effect. Without such a control, the causal claim that bidirectional context (rather than generic score averaging) drives the improvement is not fully substantiated.

The theoretical justification (Eqs. 2 and 6) is essentially a restatement that a causal model's gradient w.r.t. future tokens is zero and that averaging with a reversed pass makes it nonzero; this is definitionally true by construction and does not provide additional insight into why or when backward evaluation is informative.

All reported results appear to come from a single training run/seed (seed=1106 per Appendix A) with no variance or significance reporting across seeds or sampling runs, which is a concern for a paper making many fine-grained numerical claims (e.g., a single headline '31.9%' improvement is highlighted, which appears to be the best-case configuration rather than representative of the average gain, which is more modest, e.g., ~3-6 points absolute in several configurations).

The evaluation relies solely on downstream Best-of-N accuracy as the metric for PRM quality; no direct step-level classification metrics (e.g., accuracy/F1/AUC against gold step labels) are reported to directly validate the claim of improved verification quality, making it harder to disentangle PRM calibration improvements from artifacts of the BoN selection procedure.
The case study in Section 4.4 is a single qualitative example and offers only illustrative, not statistically rigorous, support for the claimed interpretability benefits.

No comparison to alternative or stronger external baselines beyond the paper's own L2R counterpart (e.g., other published PRM/verifier methods, or simple multi-sample self-consistency baselines) is provided, limiting the ability to contextualize the magnitude of improvement relative to the broader literature.

strengths: Very extensive empirical validation: 3 LLM backbones (1B-7B scale), 3 training objectives, 3 sampling policies, 2 solution-level benchmarks and one step-level diagnostic benchmark, totaling 54 solution-level and 12 step-level configurations, with consistent improvements throughout.

Thorough and well-designed ablations, including removing each stream individually, comparing dynamic gating vs static averaging, and (importantly) comparing against homogeneous 2xL2R/2xR2L ensembles to rule out the possibility that gains are simply due to doubled compute rather than genuine bidirectional complementarity.

Practical efficiency: the method adds negligible parameters (0.3%) and, via parallel batched execution, only ~5% inference latency overhead, which is empirically verified with wall-clock measurements rather than only theoretical FLOPs.

Insightful analysis components beyond aggregate accuracy: step-wise MAE error distributions, visualization of learned gating weight evolution across reasoning progress, and both a positive and a negative (failure) case study that meaningfully discuss when retrospective (R2L) verification helps or fails.
Clear, well-organized writing and a simple, broadly applicable framework (architecture-agnostic, objective-agnostic) that could be adopted by future PRM work.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against BiRM (Chen et al., 2025), which is explicitly identified in the introduction as the closest prior bidirectional PRM approach; the paper only argues qualitatively that BiRM is 'fundamentally forward-looking' without benchmarking against it, leaving the claimed advance over the most relevant baseline unverified.

The core mechanism (feeding a reversed step order into the same autoregressive base LLM to obtain an R2L reward) is under-justified: the paper does not clearly explain how/whether the R2L-PRM is separately fine-tuned on reversed sequences, nor discuss the training-cost implications (a full second PRM must presumably be trained for each backbone/objective combination), which is a hidden cost not reflected in the paper's efficiency claims that focus only on inference latency and gating parameters.

No variance/statistical significance reporting (e.g., across random seeds or multiple runs) despite the large number of configurations and some individually modest gains, making it hard to assess whether all reported differences are robust versus noise.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: architecturally, the method combines well-known ideas (BiLSTM-style bidirectional fusion, gating, sequence reversal) applied to PRMs; the primary innovation is the prompt-reversal implementation and the gating scheme, which is a relatively modest technical contribution.
Experimental scope is limited to mathematical reasoning tasks only (acknowledged as a limitation), so generalization to other domains such as code generation or open-ended reasoning is untested.

Case studies (Tables 5, 11, 12) are hand-picked qualitative illustrations rather than systematic quantitative error-type analysis, limiting how representative the discussed failure mode (arithmetic/algebraic skip errors) is of the model's overall weaknesses.
No code/artifact release is mentioned, which combined with underspecified R2L training details, may hinder full reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: Broad and systematic empirical evaluation spanning 3 backbones, 3 training objectives, 2 solution-level benchmarks and 1 step-level benchmark (54 + 12 configurations), with generally consistent improvements over the L2R baseline.

Useful ablations that rule out the trivial explanation that gains come purely from doubled computation: the comparison against homogeneous 2xL2R/2xR2L ensembles and static-averaging (w/o Dynamic) variants helps isolate the contribution of the bidirectional/dynamic-gating design.

Reasonably careful efficiency accounting (parameter count, theoretical FLOPs, and measured wall-clock latency under parallel execution) demonstrating the method is cheap in a specific measured deployment setting.
Illustrative qualitative case studies and a step-wise MAE/gating-weight analysis that provide some mechanistic insight into when and why the R2L stream helps.
weaknesses: Core methodological detail is under-specified and central to soundness: the paper never clearly states whether the R2L stream uses the same weights θ as the L2R stream applied out-of-distribution to a reversed step order, or whether it is separately fine-tuned on reversed-order trajectories with matching supervision. The near-identical parameter count for BiPRM vs. L2R-PRM (1.543B vs 1.548B) strongly suggests shared weights are reused for both directions, which is a substantial departure from the BiLSTM inspiration (independent forward/backward parameters) and raises real questions about whether a causal LM, never trained to process step sequences in reverse order, can produce meaningful reward signals in this regime. This ambiguity undermines both the theoretical motivation and reproducibility of the central mechanism.

The paper claims to be "the first to propose the concept of the bidirectional evaluation paradigm for PRMs," yet its own related work discusses BiRM (Chen et al., 2025) as already incorporating bidirectional/future guidance signals into PRMs. Despite positioning itself directly against BiRM's limitations, the paper never includes BiRM as an empirical baseline, which is a significant gap given it is the most directly comparable prior method.

All reported main results appear to come from a single training seed (seed=1106 is the only value listed), with no variance, standard deviation, or significance testing reported despite claiming systematic, robust gains across dozens of configurations.

Some ablation numbers raise reproducibility concerns: the 2xL2R homogeneous ensemble occasionally underperforms even the single L2R baseline (e.g., MetaMath-Mistral-7B/GSM-Plus/BCE: 50.12 for 2xL2R vs 51.90 for single L2R), which is counterintuitive for averaging two independently trained models of the same type and is not discussed or explained.

The efficiency claim of only ~5% latency overhead is measured in a narrow setting (single GPU, single solution scoring) and may not generalize to realistic high-throughput serving scenarios where doubled FLOPs would materially affect cost/throughput; this limits the broader practical significance claimed in the abstract/contributions.

Evaluation is confined entirely to mathematical reasoning (acknowledged as a limitation), so claims of general applicability to "diverse PRM architectures" and reward modeling broadly are not empirically supported outside this narrow domain.

strengths: The core idea—adding a parallel R2L evaluation stream via simple prompt/step reversal, fused with a lightweight dynamic gating module—is simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to adopt without modifying the underlying LLM.

Very extensive empirical coverage: 3 backbones of varying scale, 3 training objectives, 3 sampling policies, and 2 solution-level benchmarks plus a step-level diagnostic benchmark (54 + 12 configurations), with consistent gains throughout, which is strong evidence of robustness across settings.

Careful ablations isolate the source of improvement: removing either stream, replacing dynamic gating with static averaging, and comparing against homogeneous 2×L2R/2×R2L ensembles with matched compute budget to rule out the possibility that gains merely reflect doubled computation rather than genuine bidirectional complementarity.

Practical efficiency claims are well supported: parallel execution of the two streams keeps wall-clock latency increase to ~5% despite ~2× theoretical FLOPs, and the gating module adds negligible parameters (0.3%), making the method practically deployable.

Interpretability analysis (step-wise MAE trends and evolution of learned gating weights) provides a coherent mechanistic story for why and where L2R vs. R2L contribute differently, corroborated by qualitative case studies (including an honest failure case discussed in the appendix).
weaknesses: The paper explicitly discusses BiRM (Chen et al., 2025) as the most closely related prior bidirectional PRM work but does not include it as an experimental baseline; given the strong conceptual overlap, omitting a direct empirical comparison weakens the claimed contribution and the 'first bidirectional PRM paradigm' framing seems overstated relative to this existing work.

Implementation details of the R2L stream are under-specified: since the underlying LLM was pretrained purely autoregressively in the forward direction, it is unclear how reliably 'prompt reversal' produces meaningful representations for reversed step order (e.g., whether individual step text remains forward while only step ordering is reversed), and no sanity check/ablation validates that the reversed stream is not exploiting degenerate or spurious signals.

No variance/statistical significance reporting (e.g., across random seeds) is given for the main results despite many closely-spaced configurations, making it hard to assess whether individual comparisons (some of which show fairly small absolute gains) are reliably distinguishable from noise; the ensemble-based robustness argument partially but not fully substitutes for this.

Experimental validation is confined entirely to mathematical reasoning (as acknowledged in Limitations), so the generality of the bidirectional paradigm to other reasoning domains (code, commonsense, etc.) remains unverified.

The true training cost (need to train/host effectively two evaluation passes through the base PRM, even if weights are shared) and any additional data/compute overhead during training are not clearly quantified, only inference-time efficiency is emphasized.
